Setting up a bridge

The boards and the argument for each. Half one is getting the bridge into the house, drawn two ways; half two is getting a new switch onto the bridge — and, since a two-way is two switches and one light, saying so at setup. Every screen is 1440×900, the size of the wall.

WHY THIS EXISTS

The bridge works. Getting one does not. Today that means a laptop, a USB cable, PlatformIO, and a header file with the mesh keys pasted into it — a maker's step, in a product whose whole promise is that there is no maker's step.

Two halves, and they are not the same job:

1. GETTING THE BRIDGE IN. It needs the Wi-Fi, the hub's broker, and the keys to the switches.

2. GETTING A NEW SWITCH ONTO IT. A factory-fresh switch will not join without the 16-byte secret printed on its back, so this half has a camera in it.

Everything below is drawn on surfaces the panel already has — the sheet, the Found nearby card, New devices, room chips. Nothing here invents a screen the house has no place for.

Boards A and B are the same moment drawn two ways. They are the decision to make.

A — IT KNOCKS

The bridge arrives already knowing how to talk. Give it power anywhere in the house and it says hello over Bluetooth; the wall notices it the way it notices anything else on the network, and asks one question.

The identity check is the object, not a number. It is blinking, and you say whether the blinking thing is yours. No chip id, no serial, no "Bridge 9f2a41" on a screen in front of someone who has never seen a MAC address — and no list to pick the right one out of when two arrive at once.

FOR: nothing is ever plugged into the hub, so the hub can stay in a cupboard. One tap, from a screen you were already standing at, in the same shape as every other Found nearby moment in the house. That sameness is most of the argument.

AGAINST: it only works on a bridge that already has firmware on it. Someone put it there — either we ship them flashed, or the first one is still board B. It also needs Bluetooth on the hub: a Pi has it, most mini PCs have it, a VM may not. Which is awkward, because a hub with no Bluetooth is exactly the hub this bridge is most useful on.

B — THE CABLE, ONCE

A bare board, out of a bag, with nothing on it. Plug it into the hub's USB and the hub puts everything on it in one go: the software first, then the Wi-Fi, then the keys. The hub already reacts to a USB stick appearing and disappearing — driver-layer/radios.sh, on a udev rule — so the noticing half of this is built.

The sheet says three lines because three things happen, and none of them are words a person has to understand. "Giving it its software" is a flash. "Handing it the keys to your switches" is the part that is genuinely the house's secret, and it happens over a wire, into a thing you are holding — which is the right place for it.

FOR: works on a board with nothing on it, which is the only route that works for a bridge we did not ship. No Bluetooth, no pairing, no range, no radio at all. Nothing to type, ever — the hub already knows the Wi-Fi, the broker password and the keys.

AGAINST: a cable, and a trip to the hub. If the hub is behind the router in a cupboard, that is a real errand, and it is the only moment in this whole product that asks someone to know where the hub physically is.

NOT ACTUALLY A FORK. A and B answer different starting conditions: B is the factory, A is the doorbell. If both exist, one person only ever meets one of them, and the wall says the same sentence either way. The question to settle is which gets built first — and the answer probably depends on whether we ship pucks or people buy boards.

WHERE BOTH OF THEM END

Identical after the tap: you unplug it and walk off with it. The wall is on the wall; the phone is in your other hand and you are looking at a socket. So the thing that answers "is here good?" is the object itself.

Three states, one light. Amber blinking = looking. Green steady = it can hear your switches, leave it. Red breathing = too far. Nobody has to be taught that; you stand there until it goes green.

The phone card is for whoever wants the number, not the ritual. It is the same fact twice, and the light is the one that still works when the Wi-Fi is down — which, at that exact moment, it might be.

THE HONEST BIT: this is the only piece of half one that is firmware rather than panel, so it wants settling before anything is built. A classic ESP32 devkit has one blue LED and nothing else; the S3 has a colour one. Three colours assumes an RGB puck, or the three states become three blink rhythms on a single blue LED, which is worse and should be avoided by choosing the board.

ELEVEN SWITCHES, NAMED BY TOUCH

This is the moment the whole thing could still come out feeling like Home Assistant. Eleven rows called "Switch 000a" with a room dropdown on each is the failure mode, and it is exactly what the hub does today: all 34 entities landed under New devices in one go.

But the switches already announce themselves when a human presses them — that is proven, it is how the bridge reads state at all. So identification is free and needs no new firmware: press the switch, and the house says which row that was. You never read an address. You walk around your own house pressing things, which is a thing people already know how to do.

FOR: no naming, no guessing, no mapping hex to hallways. It degrades gracefully — all eleven work from the moment the bridge is in, so stopping halfway costs nothing but names.

AGAINST: it is a walk around the house and cannot be done from a chair. So it also has to be possible later, one switch at a time, from that switch's own tile: "Which room is this? Press it." Same mechanism, one row instead of eleven.

OPEN: a stairway's companion switch is a real mesh node with NOTHING wired to it -- it acknowledges on/off and drives no light, and telling one from the mesh now looks possible after all: field 0x13 fell to 0 when a load switched off and climbed back when it came on (16 Sep), so turning a switch on and watching 0x13 is a load detector. That was written off earlier and should be re-run before anything leans on it -- a small load may not move it. So the row says "you just pressed this one", which is true of both, and never "it came on". Also open: what a switch is called once it has a room. "Hallway — ceiling" is drawn here, but the house has no second-switch-in-a-room rule yet, and two switches in a hallway is common.

THE WALL SHOWS, THE PHONE SCANS

A factory-fresh switch will not be provisioned without the 16-byte Static OOB secret in the QR on its back. That is the mesh's own rule and it is not negotiable — it is why every No-OOB attempt failed before the QR was read (docs/brilliant.md).

So this half has a camera in it, and the wall panel does not have one. The rule that falls out of that is worth stating once and keeping: THE WALL SHOWS, THE PHONE SCANS. The wall's entire job here is the code that opens the phone on the right step, which is a pattern the panel already owns — it is how the house gets onto a phone at all (PhoneSteps.vue).

The phone then asks exactly one question, at the end: which room. Not what it is called, not whether it dims, not what kind of thing it is. The house already knows all of that from the switch itself.

WHAT THE WALL MUST NOT DO: ask anyone to type the code. It is 32 hex characters. There is no version of that which is acceptable on a screen a family walks up to, and the temptation to add it "as a fallback" should be resisted — a fallback nobody can complete is not a fallback.

TWO SWITCHES, ONE LIGHT

A two-way is two switches wired to one light. On this mesh each switch is its own node, and the one at the far end has nothing on its output at all: it acknowledges on, off and dim, and drives nothing. Show it as a device and the wall has a light that does nothing. That is the failure this pair of boards exists to prevent.

WHO KNOWS. Brilliant's own app asks for both switches BEFORE it provisions them, groups them, and does them as one job -- because the moment someone has just fitted them is the only moment they are certain which go together. We do the same, in the house's idiom: after the first code is read, one question ("does another switch work this same light?"); if yes, the second code; then both are let in together and the house writes the pairing itself. The question repeats after every switch, so three or four on one light is the same walk with one more code. Nobody is asked what a three-way is -- and nobody is told a number, because the names do not travel: two switches on one light is a "two-way" in Britain and a "3-way" in America, three is an "intermediate" or a "4-way", and the count in the name never matches the count on the wall. The house names the arrangement (one at each end) and counts the switches.

FOR SWITCHES THAT WERE HERE FIRST, the offer after a press is now the FALLBACK rather than the route. An intact pair carries its own pairing in vendor field 0x08 -- the companion stores its partner's address -- and that field reads with the AppKey alone, on switches we do not own. So the house can read every pairing in the house off the old network before it touches anything, and the press-to-offer flow is only for a pair it somehow did not see. See the two boards below.

WHAT THE HOUSE THEN DOES. On the wall it is one light. The switches are not things of their own. And a press on the far switch reaches the light BECAUSE THE TWO SWITCHES TALK TO EACH OTHER: the companion sends its partner a vendor press (0403) straight to the address in its own 0x08, and the main broadcasts its new state to all-nodes. The console is not in that path and never was -- it was watched through an intact pair's presses and issued nothing. A pair we wrote ourselves has since been pressed with no hub, no console and no panel anywhere in the loop, and the load answered. So pairing is ONE WRITE, on the companion end only, and then the house is out of it.

WHAT THIS RETIRES. An earlier version of this note said multi-way was mediated by the Brilliant console and that the hub therefore had to relay every companion press. Both halves were wrong. The relay was built (brain/hub/relay.py) and is deliberately retired: it works, and it makes a light switch that stops working when the hub reboots. The only thing it is still good for is a pair split across two networks mid-move, which is exactly the case the Alone board refuses to paper over.

WHAT IS NOT KNOWN. Whether a star of three or four companions on one main behaves like the pair we proved (n=1 on pairs, and the main appears to remember only whoever last pressed it, which may leave the other companions' own indicators wrong). And what a factory-fresh switch's 0x1b says before anyone configures it -- every switch adopted so far was previously set up by the console, so a brand-new one has no capture to replay.

WHAT HAS TO BE TRUE FOR ANY OF THIS

So the drawing is not a promise nobody can keep. In rough order of how new each one is:

BUILT ALREADY. The puck holds a proxy link and speaks the mesh with the captured keys; switches publish on touch; Home Assistant discovery makes entities without anyone naming anything. Identity is already chip id for the puck and net+addr for a switch — nothing in these boards needs a hand-typed name, which is why none of them has a text field in it.

SMALL. Naming by touch needs the hub to remember which switch reported in the last few seconds, and the panel to show it. Nothing new on the puck.

MEDIUM. Board A needs a provisioning service on the puck over BLE and something on the hub that writes to it. Board B needs esptool and a firmware image on the hub, plus the udev route radios.sh already uses for radio sticks. Either way the keys go over the wire or the link, and never onto a screen or into the panel's HTML.

THE GENUINELY NEW ONE. Half two needs the puck to act as a PROVISIONER. It is a proxy client today — it joins a network someone else made. Provisioning a switch means running the other side of the exchange the mesh-provisionee firmware currently plays the victim in, plus replaying the load-type and PIR configuration the Brilliant panel used to write (still unsolved: STATUS.md, "Own keys later"). Half one is a week of plumbing. Half two has a research question inside it, and it should not be scheduled as though it does not.

MOVING A PAIR OVER -- CARRIED, NOT RE-ASKED

This is the door this house actually walks through, and it is the one the boards above do not draw. Nine lights are already on the wall and already paired; what happens to them when the panel comes down is the whole question.

THE PAIRING IS READABLE BEFORE ANYTHING IS TOUCHED. A companion stores its partner's unicast address in vendor field 0x08, and that field answers to the AppKey alone -- no device key, which means it reads off switches we do not own, on the console's own network, without pressing anything. 0x08 is zero on a main and on a single-pole switch, and non-zero only on a companion. So the house can draw its own arrangement before the move starts: nine lights, eleven switches, two of them with a switch at each end.

WHICH MEANS THE MOVE ASKS NOTHING. Everything the setup flow has to work out by scanning two codes in a row, the migration already knows. No question about pairs, no probe to find which end has the load, no vocabulary. The name and the room survive too, because the light is the same light.

A PAIR IS ONE JOB AT TWO ENDS. Moving a switch means factory-resetting it, which is a physical ritual at the switch itself (tab out, tab in, ten seconds of finger), so a pair is two trips and the phone should say so before the first one rather than after it. Board 2 carries the pair context the whole way -- "1 of 2, the other is on the landing" -- because the failure it prevents is somebody moving one end and considering the light done.

THE PROOF IS A PRESS. After both ends land, the house rewrites the companion's 0x08 with the main's new address and asks for a press at the far end. That is the only honest confirmation available: a readback says the value is stored, and stored is not the same as live. The main broadcasts its state to all-nodes when it changes, which floods by design and arrives whichever end was touched -- so the house watches for that, and never for the companion's own position, which drifts free of the light.

WHAT IT COSTS TO BUILD. The read side is a loop over the old network's switches asking one vendor field, and the tools for it exist (tools/vendor_store.py). The write side is one field on one switch. The genuinely new work is not here at all -- it is the puck learning to provision, which half two already owes.

WHAT THE FIRST REAL READ FOUND (17 Sep, run against the house with tools/pairs.py -- read only, nothing pressed, nothing written).

THE READ ITSELF WORKS. Eleven switches on the console's network answered vendor field 0x08 over one proxy link from a laptop, with the AppKey alone. The premise of this board is no longer an argument; it is a thing that ran.

THERE ARE THREE PAIRS IN THIS HOUSE, NOT ONE. 0x0006 -> 0x0005 (the stairway, already known), 0x0016 -> 0x0002, and 0x0014 -> 0x0012. All three companions read 0x1b = 03. Two of them were news.

AND TWO OF THE THREE DO NOT POINT AT A SWITCH. 0x0002 and 0x0012 are the Control panel's own elements, and neither has a vendor store at all -- 0x0002 was asked for all 55 known fields and answered none, where every real switch answers dozens. So those two companions have the CONSOLE stored as their partner. Whatever that arrangement is (panel-mediated multi-way, or a switch set up to report to the panel), field 0x08 does not name a light, and the migration cannot carry it across silently. THE BOARD NOW SAYS SO: the hallway row is drawn as one question to ask, not as a pairing carried.

WHICH MAKES A CHEAP TEST VALUABLE. Press 0x0016 while everything is captured. If the panel answers with a Generic OnOff Set to some address, that names the light 0x0016 belongs to -- and the migration gets its answer without asking anybody after all. It also settles, for this house, whether panel-mediated multi-way is real alongside the switch-to-switch kind we proved. Nobody has ever pressed those two switches with a capture running.

THE READ-TWICE RULE EARNED ITSELF IMMEDIATELY. On pass one, 0x0014 did not answer 0x08 and would have been recorded as a main with no partner. On pass two it answered -> 0x0012. A single-pass read would have silently turned a companion into a light. That is the hazard from 'a dropped read is indistinguishable from a field that does not exist', caught on the first run that mattered.

AND THE CENSUS IS STILL PARTIAL. 0x0003, 0x000a and 0x0011 are known switches that answered nothing on either pass -- out of range of the proxy that was in reach. The tool reports them as unknown rather than as single, which is the only safe default: an unread 0x08 looks exactly like no partner. Anything built on this must walk the proxy around the house, or run from a puck that is already in the middle of it.

AND THEN THE PERSON IN THE KITCHEN CORRECTED IT (same evening). The paragraph above reads the two console-partnered companions as panel-MEDIATED multi-way. Wrong. The kitchen table light is a three-way whose third position is THE RIGHT-HAND SLIDER ON THE BRILLIANT PANEL -- 0x0012 is that slider, and 0x0014 stores it for the same reason any companion stores its main: it is the other end. It is switch-to-switch throughout; one end just lives behind glass.

WHICH IS BETTER NEWS AND WORSE NEWS. Better: there is no second arrangement to support, and the pairing can be carried after all. Worse: when the panel comes off the wall THAT END GOES WITH IT, and the kitchen drops from three switches to two. That is not a question the migration asks, it is a thing the house must SAY before anybody unscrews the panel -- and the honest offer beside it is a plate to put in its place. Neither is drawn on any board yet.

AND THE PRESS TEST NEEDS ITS OWN CORRECTION. The capture showed a press producing nothing and I read that as a dead plate. The lamp disagreed: the FIRST press did nothing, a SECOND press turned the light on. So the switch works and drops presses -- a 0403 is a directed unicast with nothing retrying it. The design consequence is small but real: any screen that says 'press the far one to check' must tolerate a press that goes nowhere, and must not conclude failure from one.

AND THE READ IS NOW PROVEN AGAINST A LAMP (17 Sep late). pairs.py had said 0x0006's partner is 0x0005, read from field 0x08 with nobody pressing anything. A controlled run on that pair -- the basement kitchen two-way, four presses, two at each end -- produced exactly the two documented signatures: the stairwell end sends 0403 and the lamp follows; the garage-door end changes the lamp and broadcasts, with no 0403 at all. The pairing this board carries across was read before anything was touched and then confirmed by a light somebody was watching.

ALSO RETIRED: THE DROPPED-PRESS WORRY. An earlier paragraph here said a confirm-by-press step must tolerate a press that goes nowhere, on the strength of the kitchen. Four for four on a healthy pair. The kitchen is a flaky install -- its own owner says so -- and three of that evening's wrong turns came from reasoning hard about single observations taken from it. Board 3's 'press the one at the other end' stands as drawn.

HALF MOVED -- AND THE SHORTCUT THAT IS REFUSED

A pair split across two networks is a pair that has stopped working: the companion is still shouting its press at an address that now lives on the other mesh. Somebody will be called away halfway up the stairs, so this state is not an edge case, it is Tuesday.

THE TEMPTATION IS REAL AND IT IS ALREADY BUILT. brain/hub/relay.py hears the companion's press on one network and commands the load on the other. It works. It was written for exactly this. And it makes a light switch whose behaviour depends on a Raspberry Pi being up -- which is the one thing in this house that must never be true. It stays retired, and this board is the reason written down.

SO THE HOUSE SAYS THE TRUE THING, IN THE ROOM IT IS TRUE IN. Not a warning banner, not a log line: the light's own row says it only answers at the bottom, and names the switch that has not come across. An unfinished light is the one thing the house brings up again on its own.

BOARD 2 IS THE ARGUMENT, NOT A SCREEN. It is drawn as a screen because that is what the canvas is made of, but no person should ever see it. It is here so the decision is visible next to the flow it constrains, and so the next person to find relay.py sitting there working does not switch it on.

THE ONE HONEST EXCEPTION worth arguing about later: a house that is mid-move for weeks rather than an evening, or one that cannot finish because a switch is behind furniture. If the relay ever comes back it should come back as a named, visible, temporary thing with an end date on it -- "carried by the hub until you finish the stairs" -- and never as an invisible default.

A NEW PAIR -- FINDING THE ONE WITH THE LAMP

Migration can read a switch's role off the old network. A switch out of a box has no such history, and the role is not cosmetic: vendor field 0x1b picks the code path, 00 drives a load and 03 routes the press outward. Write it wrong and you get the failure that cost an evening -- bound, published, partner address set, power cycled, and the switch silently applies the press to a load it has not got. So for new switches the house has to decide, and the whole design question is how it decides without using the word.

IT TRIES IT. Field 0x13 fell to 0 when a load switched off and climbed back when it came on (16 Sep). So turning each candidate on and watching 0x13 is a load detector, and it needs no new firmware -- the bridge already polls that field and already learns a floor per switch. When it works, nobody is asked anything at all: the second code is read, a few seconds pass, and the next screen is which room.

IT SAYS THE QUIET PART. The probe switches a lamp on, so a light will blink during setup. Board 1 says so rather than hoping nobody notices, because an unexplained light is alarming in a way an explained one is not.

AND WHEN IT CANNOT TELL, IT ASKS WITH A LIGHT. "Did a light just come on?" -- yes or no, one tap, no vocabulary, and both answers are equally useful. What it must never do is ask which switch is wired to the load; that is the question the whole approach exists to avoid, and most people cannot answer it about their own house.

THE FREE CATCH. If both candidates move 0x13, they are two lights and somebody answered "yes" to the pairing question when they should not have. Board 3 says so and keeps both -- nothing is lost, they are already provisioned. The escape underneath it ("No -- they are one light") is the honest admission that the detector can be right about the lamps and wrong about the house; two lamps on one circuit would read exactly this way. THAT PATH NEEDS ONE MORE SCREEN THAT IS NOT DRAWN: it has to ask which of the two the lamp is wired to, and that is the one place the horrible question is unavoidable. It should be drawn before it is built.

WHAT IS OWED BEFORE THIS IS BUILT. 0x13's resting value differs per switch (about 130 on the full-bright hallway, 285 on 0x0010, near zero on small loads), so a small load may not move it enough and the fallback may fire more often than these boards imply. One evening with a switch and a lamp settles the thresholds. Note also that the naming annotation above USED to say this test was disproved -- that was written before the 16 Sep observation, and has been corrected rather than quietly dropped.

MEASURED, 17 Sep late -- AND IT IS NOT SUBTLE. Run on the basement kitchen two-way, with the lamp switched by hand and its own OnOff broadcasts marking the transitions in the same log: dark 1-3 (n=13), lit 92-97 (n=21), dark again 2-4. Across the switch-off: 97, 97, 97 up to a second before, then 4 at two seconds after. A ~50x separation settling in about two seconds each way, with nothing near the middle.

SO BOARD 2 IS THE RARE CASE, NOT THE COMMON ONE. The house can find the switch with the lamp by trying each one and watching, and nobody is asked anything. That is the screen this design most wanted to delete, and the measurement deletes it from the normal path. It stays drawn because a fallback that is never drawn is a fallback that gets built badly.

KEY IT ON THE JUMP, NEVER THE NUMBER. Resting values differ per switch across this house -- ~130 on the full-bright hallway, 285 on 0x0010, 1-3 on this one. What identifies the load is 'this switch's own reading changed fiftyfold when I switched it', never 'this reads above 50'.

AFTERWARDS -- FROM THE LIGHT ITSELF

Setup catches the one moment somebody is holding two switches. Everything else happens later: a third switch added when a back door is fitted, a pair undone because it was wrong, a switch replaced when it dies. All of it belongs on the light's own screen, because the light is what a person goes looking for. There is no list of switches in this product and there should not be one -- a loadless companion shown as a device is a light on the wall that does nothing.

THREE AND FOUR ARE THE SAME SHAPE. Pairing is one write on the companion, naming the main's address, so a multi-way is a star: every extra switch points at the one with the lamp. Nothing about the main changes when a third is added, which is why board 2 can honestly say a fourth changes nothing either.

UNTESTED, AND IT MATTERS HERE MORE THAN ANYWHERE. We have proven one pair. The main appears to notify only whoever last pressed it, which is runtime state rather than stored configuration -- so in a four-way the other companions may hold a stale idea of the light, and if their own plate indicates state, two of the three ends would show the wrong thing. The hub does not care (it reads the main's broadcast), but a person standing at the back door does. A three-switch test is one afternoon and it should happen before this board becomes code.

TAKING ONE OFF HAS TO SAY WHAT BECOMES OF IT. Unpair a companion and it is a plate that does nothing -- so the sheet offers it a job in the same breath. "Make it a button" is not speculative: a companion reports tap (0403), slide as a signed delta, and a touch boundary, which is enough to run a scene on a tap and dim a group on a slide. It is decoded and unbuilt, and it is the reason a freed companion is worth keeping rather than forgetting.

REPLACING A DEAD ONE is the same flow with the removal and the add run back to back, and it is the case this house will hit first, since two panels have already died.

TAKING THE PANEL DOWN -- WHAT IT WAS ALSO DOING

Every other board here treats the console as a thing to be replaced. It is also a switch on a wall. The kitchen table light in this house is a three-way whose third position is the panel's right-hand slider -- confirmed by the person who lives here after a capture pointed at it. Nothing in the product knew that, and the first anyone would learn of it is a light that has quietly lost an end.

TWO LOSSES, AND ONLY ONE IS RECOVERABLE. The slider itself goes: that is physical and no software fixes it, so board 1 says it plainly, before the screwdriver rather than after. But a SECOND switch dies with it -- the wall plate whose 0x08 names a panel element has nothing to announce to once the panel is off, and a switch that announces nothing is wired to nothing. That one is one write to fix: point it at the switch the lamp is wired to, and the pair then works switch-to-switch with the house out of the path.

WHICH IS WHY THIS IS A SCREEN AND NOT A RELEASE NOTE. The fix has to happen BEFORE the panel comes off, because afterwards the house cannot tell which light that orphaned switch belonged to -- its only record of the association is a partner address that no longer answers. Do it in the wrong order and the information needed to repair it is gone with the hardware.

AND THE HOLE IS NOT A HOLE -- IT IS TWO GANGS. The panel occupies a two-gang box, and the plan for this house is to fit two ordinary Brilliant switches in its place. That is a better ending than the blank plate this board first drew: every position the panel held comes back as a real switch, on our own network, and each one is added through the flow that already exists. The kitchen ends up a genuine three-way -- one switch with the lamp, two companions pointing at it -- with no panel and no hub anywhere in the path. Strictly better than it is today.

WHICH MAKES THE ORDERING EVEN MORE LOAD-BEARING. The orphan fix still has to be written before the panel comes off, because the association is only recorded in a partner address that stops answering. But the new switches then arrive into a light the house still understands, and 'add another switch' does the rest.

WHAT IS NOT KNOWN, AND IT DECIDES WHETHER THE FIX RUNS ONCE OR TWICE. Whether the two gangs serve ONE light or TWO. 0x0014 announces to 0x0012 and 0x0016 announces to 0x0002 -- two different panel elements. If each gang is its own light, then there are two orphan fixes and two replacement switches to pair, and this screen must enumerate them. The census says it has no vendor store, like 0x0012, which is what a panel element looks like. Worth one read before this ships, because the screen has to enumerate every light the panel takes part in, not just the one we stumbled into.

KEEP THE PANEL, OR LEAVE IT -- AND WHY IT IS NOT A FORK

Two customers arrive at this product. One wants off Brilliant entirely and does not mind the panel coming out of the wall. The other has a panel whose screen still works, likes it, and wants the house to know about their switches without anything being disturbed. Every other board here was drawn for the first one.

THE SECOND IS EASIER THAN IT LOOKS, BECAUSE NOTHING HAS TO MOVE. The hub does not need a switch on ITS network to control it. With the panel network's keys a puck joins that network as one more controller, alongside the panel, and every switch appears in the house exactly as it is -- nothing reset, nothing rewired, nothing to undo. That is what the bridge in this repo already does; it was built as a stopgap and it is actually a product.

SO THE FORK IS REALLY AN ORDER. Joining is reversible and costs nothing; migrating is the better end state and can happen later, a light at a time. Only someone whose panel has already died has a single road -- and they are not asked to choose, because the question they CAN answer ('does your screen still come on?') routes them without their ever seeing a choice. That is why board 1 asks about a screen and not about networks.

WHAT KEEPING IT COSTS, SAID ON THE SCREEN RATHER THAN IN A FOOTNOTE: * STATE ARRIVES BY POLLING. Changing what a switch publishes needs its device key, which the panel holds and we will never have. A hand press shows up when we next ask. Switches already publishing to all-nodes are immediate; the rest lag. * PAIRING CAN STILL BE CHANGED. 0x08 and 0x1b are vendor fields and answer to the AppKey alone, so multi-way can be rearranged even on their network. That was a surprise and it is worth leaning on. * YOU ARE A GUEST. It rests on that panel staying alive. Two have died in this house already.

AND ONE COMBINATION NOBODY CAN HAVE: keep the panel AND move a switch over. A node cannot be evicted from the panel's mesh and still be in it, so every light that comes across DISAPPEARS from the panel's screen. Board 3 says exactly that, because it is the thing a person would otherwise discover by finding a hole in a screen they liked.

THE OPEN QUESTION THAT DECIDES WHETHER ANY OF THIS SHIPS. The keys were captured here by flashing a recorder and adding it through THE BRILLIANT APP. Scenario two's whole premise is a customer whose panel still works -- so does that provisioning still succeed with Brilliant's servers unreachable? If it needs their cloud, this path has a shelf life set by somebody else's decisions, and that belongs in the decision before anybody builds it.
